entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Robert III of Loritello, also known as Robert of Bassunvilla, was a powerful Norman count in the Kingdom of Sicily, who died in 1182. As Count of Loritello and Conversano, he commanded significant feudal lands across Apulia and Abruzzo, making him a pivotal figure in the volatile political landscape of Southern Italy during the reigns of Kings William I and William II. His career exemplifies the complex relationship between the Norman monarchy and its powerful baronial class, marked by both fierce rebellion and strategic service. His family, originating from Vassonville near Dieppe in Normandy, had established a formidable presence in the Mezzogiorno, contributing to the consolidation and intermittent destabilization of the nascent Sicilian kingdom.

Robert's most prominent actions involved his participation in a major baronial revolt against King William I in 1156. This rebellion, fueled by resentment over royal centralization and perceived tyrannical rule, saw Robert as a leading conspirator alongside other powerful nobles. Though initially successful in challenging royal authority and even briefly driving William I from Palermo, the revolt ultimately failed, leading to Robert's exile to Constantinople by 1161. He leveraged his connections within the Byzantine court, and with the death of William I in 1166, Robert was able to return to Sicily, playing a crucial role in the regency council for the young King William II and subsequently becoming a trusted advisor.
